content: An adduct, derived from the Latin term adductus meaning drawn toward, refers to a chemical product formed through the direct addition of two or more distinct molecules. This process results in a single reaction product that incorporates all the atoms from the participating components. The formation of an adduct involves the creation of two chemical bonds and a net reduction in bond multiplicity in at least one of the reactants. The resulting compound is considered a unique molecular species. For example, an adduct is formed when hydrogen peroxide reacts with sodium carbonate, producing sodium percarbonate. Another example is the reaction between sodium bisulfite and an aldehyde, which yields a sulfonate. Adducts are frequently observed in interactions between Lewis acids and Lewis bases. A notable example is the formation of adducts between the Lewis acid borane (BH₃) and the oxygen atom in Lewis bases such as tetrahydrofuran (THF) or diethyl ether, resulting in compounds like BH₃·THF and BH₃·OEt₂. Adducts are not exclusively molecular in nature. In solid-state chemistry, adducts can form between gases and solid compounds. For instance, ethylene or carbon monoxide can form adducts with CuAlCl₄. In this case, the solid CuAlCl₄, which has an extended lattice structure, incorporates the gas molecules as ligands bound to the copper atoms within the lattice. This process results in the formation of a new extended phase where the gas molecules are integrated into the structure. The formation of such adducts can also be interpreted as a reaction between a base and a Lewis acid. In this context, the copper atom acts as the electron-accepting species (the Lewis acid), while the π-electrons of the gas molecules serve as the electron-donating species (the base).
